message:
feat(grammar): native grammars are the default JavaScript parsers

JSON, INI, Diff, CSV, JSON5, Scheme and Racket now parse with their native
merged grammar and automatic error recovery. The catalog lists the native
grammar first in grammars and the tree-sitter grammars in oracleGrammars;
the projection keeps the oracle's default CST rows for valid input.

feat(grammar): native grammars are the default Rust parsers

Port of the JavaScript native default parse: parse_programming_language,
embedded regions and incremental reparses run the catalog's native grammar
for the seven native languages. The crate ships src/data/native-grammars,
exports native_grammars and oracle_grammar_provenance, and the default CST
suite checks native rows against the pinned oracle.
docs(grammar): document the native default parse

build(grammar): native languages' tree-sitter oracles are development dependencies

JSON, INI, Diff, CSV, JSON5, Scheme and Racket parse with their native
grammars by default, so their tree-sitter grammars move out of both
packages:

- Rust: tree-sitter-json, -ini, -diff, -json5-orchard, -racket and
  -scheme are [dev-dependencies]; the vendored CSV parser is neither
  compiled by build.rs nor published (the crate LICENSE include is
  anchored to the root so no vendored LICENSE leaks in). grammar_by_id
  and grammar_names return None for the oracle ids, and each native
  suite gains a pinned_*_oracle_gives_the_fixture test that parses the
  corpus with the oracle crate.
- JavaScript: the oracle wasm builds and licenses move to
  js/oracles/grammars, outside the npm package, with their own NOTICE;
  the lock entries carry "oracle": true and grammarNames returns
  undefined for them. The fixture generator, oracle checks and
  inventory locate them through js/scripts/grammar-files.mjs.

The dependency inventory and audit are updated offline
(experiments/issue-195-oracle-dev-dependency-inventory.mjs); a package
release test asserts the oracles are development files only.
I195-DEPENDENCY-PRODUCTION-PARSERS-REMOVED stays open until the
remaining languages parse natively.

fix(ci): keep Rust tests out of src and give the dependency refresh a read-only default

The Rust workflow failed at a993919:
- Lint rejected the #[cfg(test)] module in src/native_grammar_parser.rs.
  The table check moves to tests/unit/default_cst_expectations.rs (the
  catalog's native grammars are exactly the shipped files); the default
  CST suite already checks each native parse and its recovery.
- workflow_security rejected dependency-refresh.yml: the workflow now
  defaults to contents: read with the shared pull-request-only
  cancellation group, and only the refresh job gets write permissions,
  in a non-cancelling write queue.
fix(issue-195): refresh the manifest digest of the regenerated dependency inventory

feat(grammar): rules carry a concept id and their source names in the links form

A rule link takes (concept ID), the canonical concept record the rule means,
and (source-names (SOURCE NAME)...), the names it has in the grammars it was
merged from, between the action and the doc, in both runtimes.
feat(grammar): native default trees keep the tree-sitter kind of renamed rules

feat(grammar): native grammar rules have English names and a concept id

Inherited names that are not English words are renamed (_value to value,
_datum to datum, sexp_comment to datum_comment, regex to
regular_expression, lang_name to language_name, linerange to line_range,
...). A renamed rule keeps its tree-sitter name as a source-name alias, so
the default tree keeps the oracle's node kinds.

feat(naming): every native grammar rule has a concept record, shared or language-specific

The 72 concepts the native grammars introduce get records with
definitions; every record a native grammar uses carries one
native:<language> source alias per rule. check:naming covers native
rule names and concept references, and ten new lookalike distinctions
keep data-format and reader constructs apart.

feat(grammar): native constructs translate through shared concept records, with a per-language reuse report

Both runtimes check that every native grammar rule names a concept record
whose native:<language> aliases are exactly its rules, compute the per-language
report of shared and language-specific rules (published in
docs/grammar/native-grammar-concept-reuse.md and checked by
npm run check:concept-reuse), and translate construct trees between native
grammars through the concept records alone.

test(issue-195): shared concepts, reuse report, concept translation and native rule names are ledger rows

New rows I195-GRAMMAR-SHARED-CONCEPTS, I195-GRAMMAR-CONCEPT-REUSE-REPORT,
I195-GRAMMAR-CONCEPT-TRANSLATION and I195-NAMING-NATIVE-GRAMMARS from the
green-path audit, each observed by JavaScript and Rust tests over
parity/fixtures/grammar-shared-concepts.json.

ci(issue-195): install JavaScript dependencies before packing delivery candidates

The evidence runner imports the language catalog builder, which parses
native grammar source names with links-notation, so the Delivery
Candidates job failed with ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND.

experiment(issue-195): tree-sitter grammar.json converts to an executable native grammar

js/experiments/tree-sitter-native-convert.mjs imports a tree-sitter
grammar.json into native Links Notation with no regular expression left:
patterns compile into classes, sequences and repeats, precedences into
precedence forms, and the word rule into keyword extraction. The imported C
grammar gives tree-sitter-c's exact trees on four real C files.

feat(grammar): tree-sitter grammar.json imports as an executable native grammar

importTreeSitterNative turns every grammar.json construct into a native
expression, extracts keywords as tree-sitter does (every token whose texts
the word token matches), and renames rules through nameOf. The native C
grammar it produces builds the tree-sitter-c trees of six real C files in
both runtimes (JS 30-750 ms, Rust 13-140 ms per file).

feat(grammar): (matching longest) gives a tie to the parse with the longer token

Tree-sitter's lexer takes the longest token, so an imported tree-sitter grammar
must prefer, of two parses alike in cost and dynamic precedence, the one whose
first differing token is longer. Both executors walk the two results' leaves in
order, skipping trivia and shared subtrees; at the first differing leaf pair the
leaf ending later wins, and a pair ending alike keeps the ambiguity.

The ambiguity feature of the feature union fixture declares matching longest,
parses l:-1 as one token, and a second mutation shows that without it the parse
is ambiguous; both runtimes run the case.

feat(grammar): a lower-precedence edge child invalidates a result only when it conflicts

A precedence filter rejected f(a)->t in C: the call (prec 15) is the
leftmost child of the field access (prec 16), though tree-sitter sees no
LR conflict there because the call's last child, the argument list, can
never be the field access operand. An edge child of lower precedence now
invalidates a result only when its own child facing the operator has a
kind the operand on that edge can match as one child; an unknown operand
keeps the strict rule. Both runtimes agree; the feature-union fixture
pins 1().2 (stands) beside 1+2.3 (the (1+2).3 parse is rejected).

feat(grammar): recovery continues after a MISSING leaf once per offset

A sequence that continues after a zero-width MISSING leaf at a repair point
may repair what follows, but a second such continuation inside it at the same
offset is matched quietly, and calls inside the first are memoized apart.
Chains of MISSING leaves made nearly every C rule left-recursive at the
end-of-input repair point, so one repair round needed more than 50M steps;
each round now takes about 10-17k. The json5 tree for {"a" 1} becomes the
cheaper (MISSING ":") value:(number "1").

feat(grammar): (matching longest) orders conflicting tokens as a lexer does

Under (matching longest) two results that end at the same offset in the
same state and differ only in a token now keep the token a tree-sitter
lexer would choose: higher lexical precedence, then the longer token,
then the more specific token (a literal over a pattern, an immediate
token over a separated one), then the token declared first. A token
also wins over a skipped separator it covers, and a terminal may match
at the start of a skipped anonymous trivia leaf (a "\n" token that an
extra would otherwise swallow).

The precedence filter takes the kinds of an optional or a repetition
from its item, so a lower-precedence operand nested in an optional edge
child is seen.

Both runtimes rank tokens when they load the program. The feature union
fixture covers the keyword-over-identifier, the token-over-separator and
the optional-edge cases with mutations that drop (matching longest), and
its generator keeps the recorded interchange section.

feat(grammar): a literal that takes the separators after it keeps its name

Under (matching longest) a literal token matched before a separator it
covers also takes each next separator it matches (`\n\n` is one `\n`
token, as in a tree-sitter lexer). Its leaf is now an anonymous alias of
the literal (`'\n` over `\n\n`) instead of an unnamed leaf named by its
text, so the C preprocessor line `#if A(B || C) && !D(F)` followed by a
blank line has the `\n` token the tree-sitter oracle reports.

The feature union fixture records the `n:1\n\n2` case; both runtimes
build the same tree.

feat(grammar): keyword lexing under (matching longest) as a tree-sitter lexer does

A tree-sitter lexer takes a keyword (a literal closed by a word-character
lookahead) over a conflicting token wherever the keyword is valid, so a
keyword such as `typedef` or `if` is never an identifier where it could
also be the keyword. Under (matching longest) both executors now do the
same:

- a parse records the spans where a keyword matched in syntactic context
  and marks the leaves of token rules (an alias keeps the token rule's kind);
- after a successful parse, a token leaf over such a span that the keyword
  outranks makes the span keyword-only, and the parse (with its repair)
  runs again with a fresh step budget until no new span appears;
- a token rule does not match a keyword-only span the keyword outranks.

The feature union's ambiguity feature gains `w:do;`, which is rejected
only with (matching longest), and docs/grammar/feature-union.md
describes keyword lexing.

feat(grammar): settle LR conflicts as a generated tree-sitter parser does

Three rules of both executors, which the native C grammar needs to parse
its corpus without ambiguities:

- A silent rule named by a `conflict` declaration builds no node to carry
  an ambiguity, so its results are not ambiguous (`a;` is a use or a
  declaration of one silent `item`).
- Complete results end apart before their trailing trivia, so they are
  ranked as a result set ranks results with one end: the cost, then under
  `matching longest` the tokens a lexer prefers and the shift order, then
  the dynamic precedence. The parse is ambiguous only on a tie.
- Under `matching longest`, a tie the tokens cannot settle goes to the
  shift or reduction an LR parser keeps: at the first nodes of one kind
  from one offset that end apart, the higher precedence level wins, and on
  equal levels a right-associative node shifts on and a left one reduces.

The ambiguity feature of the feature-union fixture gains the c:, p: and g:
cases and their mutations; docs/grammar/feature-union.md specifies the rules.

feat(grammar): native C grammar from the automatic merge pipeline

js/scripts/import-native-grammars.mjs is the automatic merge pipeline
(I195-MERGE-AUTOMATIC-PIPELINE): it imports each pinned upstream grammar
of parity/grammars/sources.json, checked by hash, as an executable native
grammar, names the rules in English through
parity/naming/grammar-name-expansions.json (the reviewed decisions), gives
every rule a concept record, states whether native grammars share it or
only one language defines it, and writes the merge report of each
language. `npm run check:native-imports` fails on drift.

The first imported language is C, from tree-sitter-c 0.24.2:
parity/grammars/native/c.lino parses the 100 sources of the upstream corpus
the oracle accepts into the oracle's rows, with no ambiguity, and rejects
the 30 the oracle recovers from, in JavaScript and Rust. The catalog lists
the native grammar first and the default parse projects its trees onto the
oracle's rows; the concept reuse report, the shared constructs and the
default CST expectations include C.

build(grammar): tree-sitter-c is a development dependency

C parses with its native merged grammar by default, so tree-sitter-c moves
out of both packages, as the other native languages' oracles did:

- Rust: tree-sitter-c is a [dev-dependency] that
  pinned_c_oracle_gives_the_fixture loads; grammar_by_id and grammar_names
  return None for the c oracle id.
- JavaScript: c.wasm.gz and its license move to js/oracles/grammars,
  outside the npm package; the lock entry carries "oracle": true.

The Rust recovery suite gains C (the JavaScript one lists every native
grammar already), the package release test lists the C oracle, and the
dependency inventory and audit are updated offline
(experiments/issue-195-oracle-dev-dependency-inventory.mjs).

docs(grammar): record the native C grammar and the import pipeline

docs/grammar/native-grammars.md gains an Imported grammars section on
js/scripts/import-native-grammars.mjs (pinned sources checked by hash,
English names from the reviewed expansions, concept records, merge
reports, check:native-imports) and the C sources, conflict settling,
fixture counts and limits; the README, the vision status and a changelog
fragment list C, and the acceptance manifest is refreshed.

feat(grammar): settle precedence like a generated LR parser and keep structured extras

Both runtimes now resolve precedence between a reduction and a shift the way a
generated tree-sitter parser does: a lexed shift, reachability of the owning
rule, the reduction tail of silent rules and the rank of lexical precedence
leaves. An extra that names a normal rule becomes a trivia node, rendered
~(kind ...), so a structured comment keeps its tree. The feature union gains
the structured-extra case and its mutation in both runtimes.

refactor(grammar): split the Rust executor below the file size limit

executor.rs (1629 lines) and results.rs (1080 lines) exceeded the 1000-line
limit the Rust lint job enforces. Trivia, terminals and tokens move to
lexing.rs, the precedence filter to precedence.rs, and the order of results of
one end and state to ordering.rs; behavior is unchanged.

fix(grammar): divide corpus cases at the longest line of dashes like tree-sitter test

A source may hold shorter --- lines (Cargo script frontmatter), so the first
dash line truncated it into a false oracle error.

feat(grammar): import the pinned tree-sitter-rust grammar with its native scanner

The import pipeline reads a source's native scanner file, checked against
its pinned sha256, and imports the externals the scanner reads from the
current byte under immediateToken. tree-sitter-rust 0.24.2 (77a3747 and
the oracle's meta-language.patch) is pinned with its corpus and license;
parity/grammars/scanners/rust.lino ports src/scanner.c. The naming
decisions expand the Rust abbreviations after The Rust Reference.

feat(grammar): keep the tree-sitter names of node kinds only an alias names

A (kind NAME (source-names ...)) link records the upstream name of a node
kind no rule defines, such as tree-sitter-rust's doc_comment, which an
alias names. Both runtimes read and write it; the catalog counts it among
the oracle kinds; the native import emits it.

perf(grammar): scan past a failing element once per repair point

Error recovery reparses with one more repair point per round. At a repair
point, a failing element yields a MISSING leaf and an ERROR leaf that skips
to the next offset where the element matches again. Two error.txt cases of
the tree-sitter-rust corpus repeated that skip scan for the same element,
offset and state (1835 scans, 59 distinct) and ran out of the step budget.
Both runtimes now keep each scan per executor, so the cases recover and
the repaired trees stay the same.

fix(grammar): settle reduce/reduce conflicts by precedence and same-tree ties

A node reduced alone under a precedence keeps its level, and of two
results ending together the one whose chain reduces at the higher level
wins, as tree-sitter resolves a reduce/reduce conflict statically (Rust's
m!(x); is an expression statement, not a macro declaration). Two results
that build the same trees are no longer an ambiguity.

feat(grammar): parse Rust with the native merged grammar by default

parity/grammars/native/rust.lino, imported with its ported scanner, is the
default Rust parse in both runtimes. parity/fixtures/native-grammars/rust.json
checks it against tree-sitter-rust on 170 matches and 35 rejections with no
ambiguity; the ledger row I195-GRAMMAR-NATIVE-RUST tracks both suites. The
native default CST expectations give the native rows of embedded regions in
a native language, so the Markdown fenced Rust recovery region is the native
repair. Rust names the shared comment, block comment, character and escape
concepts.

test(grammar): the Rust recovery suite covers the native Rust grammar

The Rust suite now repairs every rejection of the native Rust fixture, as
the JavaScript one does for every native grammar; the ledger row names all
nine native fixtures.

build(grammar): tree-sitter-rust is a development oracle only

Rust parses with its native merged grammar by default, so the patched
tree-sitter-rust parser moves out of both packages, as CSV's did:

- Rust: build.rs no longer compiles vendor/tree-sitter-rust and the crate
  no longer publishes it; grammar_by_id and grammar_names return None for
  "rust". The Rust suites check the executor against the fixture rows.
- JavaScript: rust.wasm.gz and its license move to js/oracles/grammars,
  outside the npm package; the lock entries carry "oracle": true and both
  NOTICE tables are regenerated.

The dependency inventory and audit are updated offline
(experiments/issue-195-oracle-dev-dependency-inventory.mjs), and the
vendored CSV and Rust parser notices say they are oracles.

fix(grammar): tree-sitter \s imports as ASCII white space

tree-sitter compiles `\s` to [ \t\n\v\f\r], not to the Unicode set of
JavaScript; the pinned Rust and C oracles report an ERROR on a no-break
space (js/experiments/tree-sitter-whitespace-class.mjs). The native C and
Rust grammars skipped NBSP, BOM, U+2028/2029 and Zs as extras, so three
generative Rust cases parsed clean where the oracle has errors. Both
fixtures now reject those separators in both runtimes.

perf(grammar): left recursion grows from the results of the last pass only

Each grow pass re-derived the rule body from every seed, so an operator
chain of n links cost n passes of n seeds and rustc's weird-exprs.rs ran
out of steps. A pass now seeds only the results the pass before added or
changed; a tie with a tree of an earlier pass is marked ambiguous where
the rule body marks it. Both runtimes keep every fixture tree.

fix(grammar): LR-like choices for closures in or-patterns and nested ranges (JS)

Two nodes from one offset with differing leftmost chains part where one
reduced and the other shifted; a bare range has no operand the operator
could take instead; a node nested first in the other parse's node is
entered alone until the two line up. Probes for row differences, order
traces, shrinking and punch_card growth come with it.

perf(grammar): a lone right operand stands only where no reduction ends before it (JS)

A bare range as the right operand of a range at its level is what an LR
parser shifts only when nothing reduces at the operator (`a ..= ..`, not
`.. ..` or `a .. ..`): keeping the others multiplied the parses of
punch_card past the step budget of weird-exprs.rs.
fix(grammar): the Rust executor settles closures in or-patterns and nested ranges as the JS one does
test: package and lazy-loading checks follow the native Rust grammar

body:
## Next phase: JavaScript first, automated grammars, self-translation to Rust — audit of `11d87be7`, 2026-10-04

[The previous requirements comment](https://github.com/link-foundation/meta-language/pull/196#issuecomment-5965533606) stays in force. This comment adds the maintainer's new working requirements and records the state after the 48 commits since `6f727a4d`. Implementation is already authorized: do not ask for approval, scope decisions or credentials, and do not stop.

### Delivered since the last audit (keep it)

- PR checks now depend only on pre-merge state (`1f3ec228`), and npm publishing moved to the release tag with trusted-publisher verification (`84f76331`).
- Both native executors recover from errors automatically (`72db94b6`, `e720e20d`), and native grammars are now the default parsers (`f9033f48`, `7809cf79`).
- Native grammar rules have English names and concept ids, and every rule has a shared or language-specific concept record (`ed8b9f39`, `1974f9a4`). Shared constructs translate through concepts, with a per-language reuse report (`2055ad80`).
- Tree-sitter `grammar.json` imports as an executable native grammar (`bb8b355b`). That import feeds the **native C** grammar (`adb93e5a`) and the **native Rust** grammar with its scanner (`e91ccbef`, `7a6e4dc5`).
- 9 catalog languages now have native grammars.

### 0. Fix the current red checks first, in one batch

At `c72f9cd2` (the last completed run; `11d87be7` is still running, and its `JavaScript Tests (tooling)` job has already failed):

- **Rust**, failing in Test (translation and remaining, on all three OSes), Code Coverage, Fresh Merge Simulation and Lint. The test results show `815 passed; 4 failed`:
  - `error_recovery_parity::malformed_input_recovers_to_the_same_tree_as_the_native_tree_sitter_runtime` (`tests/unit/error_recovery_parity.rs:20`)
  - `issue_195_generative::issue_195_generative_fixtures_record_their_seed_and_oracle_and_the_seed_regenerates_their_inputs` (`:124`)
  - `issue_195_generative::issue_195_generative_rust` (`:409`)
  - `issue_195_conformance::issue_195_conformance_rust` (`:312`)
- **JavaScript:** the grammar, downstream and conformance test groups fail.
- **Formal AI Workloads** fails, and **Full Requirements Aggregate** is at `276/293, 2 gate errors`.

These failures appeared when native parsing became the default. The tests still expect the **tree-sitter runtime's** trees. **Do not revert to tree-sitter.** Make tree-sitter the **oracle**: compare the native trees against it, and record every justified discrepancy as the native grammar suites already do. Then the conformance, generative and recovery suites test the native parser.

### 1. Rely on automated grammar import, conversion, merging and transformation

- **Tree-sitter must not be a required dependency.** Its trees are read-only: you cannot transform a tree-sitter CST or AST and emit source again. **Editable CSTs and ASTs that can be transformed and emitted are the core of this system.** Every parse, transformation and emission must run on our own links representation.
- Status:
  - JavaScript: `web-tree-sitter` is **still a production dependency**.
  - Rust: `rust/Cargo.toml` still has **45 `tree-sitter*` crates in `[dependencies]`**, and 7 in dev-dependencies.
  - 9 of the 70 non-natural-language catalog entries have a native grammar.
- **Generate the remaining grammars in bulk with the automated pipeline. Do not write them one by one by hand.**
  1. Run the `grammar.json` importer **and** the ANTLR grammars-v4 importer over every catalog language in one batch.
  2. Merge each language's sources.
  3. Publish a matrix of which languages import, execute and match their oracle, and which executor or scanner features each one is missing.
  4. Implement each missing feature **once, generically** (lexical modes, indentation and layout, heredocs, raw strings, nested comments, context-sensitive lexing), then regenerate every grammar.
- Express adjustments as **recorded, data-driven transformation rules** applied by the pipeline, never as hand edits of generated grammars. The LR-style conflict settling added recently (`9a66bf55`, `87c2103c`, `96d17e8e`) must be declared grammar data that the ANTLR and PEG importers can use too. It must not be behavior hard-coded in the host code for tree-sitter alone.
- Grammar transformations are part of the product. That means import, export, conversion, merging, renaming, deduplication, left-recursion handling and precedence lowering, all with public APIs and CLI commands in both packages.

### 2. JavaScript/TypeScript first, then Rust, by automated translation

- **Develop every feature in JavaScript first, and fix all of its bugs there.** JavaScript gives faster development, and builds and test runs are cheap. **Only when a feature is complete and green in JavaScript, port it to Rust in one batch.** Then check that the Rust version behaves exactly the same.
- The current history ports every small fix by hand, commit by commit: for example `429ff765` (JS), then `11d87be7` (Rust). That doubles the work and the build time. Stop doing it.
- **Use meta-language to translate itself.** Build a utility, available as both a library API and a CLI in both packages:
  - It reads JavaScript or TypeScript into meta-language links and writes Rust, and the reverse, Rust to JavaScript/TypeScript.
  - Port the `js/src` modules to `rust/src` with it, and keep porting everything with it as far as possible. Generated Rust must pass `cargo check`, clippy and the shared parity corpus.
  - Code that cannot be translated yet is a gap in the translator to fix, not something to write by hand.
- **Expand the scope to full program translation through meta-language:** JavaScript/TypeScript ↔ Rust for real modules, not only the fixture subset. The current 12 directed pairs remain required. Treat **meta-language's own source code as the main acceptance corpus.**
- **Lossless round trips** are the target:
  - JS → links → JS and Rust → links → Rust are byte-identical;
  - JS → Rust → JS and Rust → JS → Rust preserve behavior;
  - comments, layout and names are kept through provenance wherever the target can express them.
- **Reuse the experience of [RML PR #184](https://github.com/link-foundation/relative-meta-logic/pull/184):**
  - RML keeps its JavaScript and Rust implementations equal with **one shared corpus**. Its expected outputs live in Links Notation (`examples/expected.lino`), and `scripts/check-corpus-parity.mjs` runs every example in both runtimes and compares exit status, stdout and stderr.
  - RML also exports to Lean, Rocq, JavaScript and Rust.
  - Apply the same contract here: every translated module has shared corpus cases whose expected outputs are written in Links Notation and checked in both runtimes.
- **Provide exactly all features in both packages.** `parity/language-features.json` must list every public JavaScript feature. A test fails when Rust lacks one, and when the two produce different observable output for one.

### 3. Make everything extensible with decorators

- Every level accepts **decorators** that wrap and extend the default behavior without editing the core:
  - importer
  - grammar rule
  - merge decision
  - concept mapping
  - executor and recovery
  - CST → AST lowering
  - transformation
  - emitter
  - translation rule
- Decorators compose in a defined order. Store them as **links data** wherever possible, so that the JavaScript and Rust packages share one set of rules.
- **Use decorators to make translated code match the current hand-written source** in both languages: naming, error types, ownership and borrowing, module layout, formatting. Measure the difference between the translated output and the existing `rust/src` (and `js/src`) for each module, publish it, and drive it toward zero.
- **Tests:**
  - a decorator works at every level;
  - composition order is deterministic;
  - removing a decorator restores the default output;
  - decorators loaded from links data behave the same in both runtimes.

### 4. Reminder: features still missing

The open rows from the previous comment remain required. Keep them in view while the grammar work proceeds:

- **Native grammars:**
  - `I195-GRAMMAR-NATIVE-MERGED` and `I195-GRAMMAR-LANGUAGE-CATALOG`: 61 entries remain.
  - `I195-GRAMMAR-LOSSLESS-TREES` and `I195-GRAMMAR-DEPENDENCY-BOUNDARY`.
  - `I195-DEPENDENCY-PRODUCTION-PARSERS-REMOVED`: `web-tree-sitter` and 45 Rust crates are still production dependencies.
- **Merging:** `I195-MERGE-AUTOMATIC-PIPELINE`, `I195-MERGE-SHIPPED-GRAMMARS-ARE-MERGED`, `I195-MERGE-QUALITY-EVIDENCE` (coverage, correctness, recovery, time and memory against independent sources).
- **Oracles:** `I195-ACCEPTANCE-INDEPENDENT-ORACLES`, using tree-sitter, ANTLR and official compilers on real projects.
- **Interchange:** `I195-INTERCHANGE-FORMAT-FEATURES` and `I195-INTERCHANGE-CROSS-FORMAT-TOOLS`, checked with the actual target tools.
- **Semantics and downstream:**
  - `I195-SEMANTICS-CONSTRUCT-INVENTORY`: the full JavaScript, Rust, Lean and Rocq construct inventory, with normal JavaScript accepted without annotations.
  - `I195-DOWNSTREAM-TYPESCRIPT-TRANSLATIONS`: formal-ai's projection pairs on clean candidate installs.
- **Shared concepts:**
  - Grow the shared concept library family by family, as listed in the previous comment.
  - Every construct that is 1:1 across three or more languages resolves to one concept identity.
  - Lookalike concepts stay distinct.
- **Release:** after merge, CI on `main` publishes npm and the crate. npm still serves only `0.46.0`.

### 5. Minimize waiting, and work in bulk

- **Never sit idle waiting for CI.** After a push, continue with the next unfinished item: the next language family, the next translator gap, the next decorator level. Collect the CI results at the next batch boundary, and fix **all** reported failures in one batch.
- **Bulk changes:**
  1. Draft every change of a batch.
  2. Commit locally, re-read the full diff and fix it.
  3. **Push only when the batch is fully drafted.**
- Prefer automated changes (generators, importers, the translator, codemods) over many manual edits.
- **Resources.** Earlier sessions were killed for running out of memory (exit 137):
  - Run only targeted JavaScript tests locally, plus one `cargo check` when porting, with `CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=2 RUST_TEST_THREADS=2 CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0`.
  - Never run the full acceptance pipeline, the toolchain matrix, consumer installs, coverage or whole-corpus runs locally.
  - Run `node scripts/clean-caches.mjs` after every batch, and kill leftover `cargo`, `rustc`, `node`, `lean` and `rocq` processes.

### 6. CI follows the same order: JavaScript first, then Rust; and it reports every failure

**Rust CI must never start until JavaScript CI has fully passed.** Today `js.yml`, `rust.yml` and `issue-195-acceptance.yml` all start in parallel on every push. Rust builds and runs its matrix even when JavaScript is already red, which wastes runner time and buries the real failure.

- Put the JavaScript jobs and the Rust jobs in **one workflow**, with every Rust job (`cargo check` gate, tests, MSRV, lint, coverage, fresh merge, build) declaring `needs:` on the final JavaScript job. Alternatively, trigger Rust with `workflow_run` when JavaScript completes successfully. Either way, keep the check names the ruleset requires valid.
- The same order applies inside the acceptance workflow. Rust evidence stages, Rust native translations and Rust consumers run only after the JavaScript stages pass.
- Rust jobs that are skipped because JavaScript failed must appear as **skipped**, not failed, so the report points at the JavaScript failure.
- A repository test fails if any Rust job can start without a successful JavaScript prerequisite.

**Inside each job, every failure must be reported in one run, not only the first.** The matrices already use `fail-fast: false`. Within jobs, the first failure still hides the rest:

- **The `js.yml` checks job** runs about 20 sequential `npm run check:*` steps: parity, default CST, native imports, native grammars, concept records, concept reuse, issue 195, dependencies, naming, documentation and others. None has `if: ${{ !cancelled() }}`, so the first failing check skips all the others. Add `if: ${{ !cancelled() }}` to every check step, or run them all through one script that prints every failure and exits non-zero at the end.
- **Rust:** `cargo test --all-features --tests` (`rust.yml:595`) stops after the first failing test binary, so add `--no-fail-fast`. In the lint job, run `cargo fmt --check`, clippy and `cargo doc` independently so that each reports its result.
- Each acceptance evidence stage and the evaluator must still run and report when another stage fails.
- **Test the workflow structure:** a repository test fails if a check step lacks the always-run condition, or if `cargo test` lacks `--no-fail-fast`.

### 7. Record all of this in the documentation and validate it with tests

- Add these requirements to `docs/vision.md`, `AGENTS.md` and `CONTRIBUTING.md`:
  - JavaScript-first, then Rust;
  - self-translation and lossless round trips;
  - automated grammar pipeline instead of hand work;
  - tree-sitter only as a test oracle;
  - decorators at every level;
  - bulk changes and no idle waiting;
  - resource limits;
  - CI that runs Rust only after JavaScript passes;
  - CI that reports every failure.
- Register **this comment** in `parity/issue-195-sources.json`, and add atomic ledger rows, each with JS and Rust tests where applicable. At minimum:
  - the self-translation tool (JS/TS → Rust and Rust → JS/TS) as a library API and CLI;
  - lossless round trips;
  - translated modules matching the hand-written source;
  - one decorator API at every level;
  - feature-parity completeness;
  - no production tree-sitter dependency for any native language;
  - bulk import of every catalog grammar;
  - CI workflow structure: Rust jobs gated on JavaScript success, `--no-fail-fast`, always-run check steps.

**Completion** is still: every PR check green, every requirement row passing, and a release from `main` after merge.

message: test: the generative manifest records the current conformance manifest hash
fix(grammar): a recovered MISSING leaf comes before the white space it follows, as in tree-sitter
experiments: list and show native Rust recovery trees that differ from the oracle

fix(grammar): no recovery skip ends at an external scanner token, as in tree-sitter

A scanner such as a Rust string's content reads to the end of the input
before it fails, so scanning for a skip that ends at it from every later
offset was quadratic and ran a few-kilobyte Rust file with one stray byte
out of its step budget, leaving one ERROR over the whole input. Tree-sitter
lexes the skipped input in its error state, where the scanner refuses to
run, so it never resumes at such a token either. The JS and Rust executors
skip alike; a regression test in both covers the case.
experiments: bisect the step budget of a native recovery and show recovery limits

fix(grammar): recovery repairs a later error where it is instead of skipping the input after an earlier one

When the cheapest complete result of a repair round takes the rest of the
input as ERROR at a repair point, while the result that reaches farthest
ends past it and could still complete for less with one more repair, the
round asks for that end as the next repair point; the complete result
stands when the rounds end. The JS and Rust executors defer alike; three
native fixture recoveries skip fewer bytes, and twenty Rust conformance and
generative recoveries become local.
fix(grammar): the recovered rest of the input leaves the final white space out of its ERROR, as in tree-sitter
fix(grammar): a MISSING keyword is named by its literal, as in tree-sitter
test(conformance): record each native recovery that differs from the oracle with a justified category
test(conformance): the Rust suites check each recorded native recovery as the JS suites do
test: the requirement manifest records the current generative manifest hash
test(recovery): an error-recovery case with a native recovery record is checked by its record
chore(deps): the dependency inventory lists the native recovery generator
test(conformance): the native recovery record check asserts a non-empty case list as clippy asks

feat(grammar): named precedences ranked by declared orders and a scanner condition on what the parse expects, as in tree-sitter

A precedence named by a string (namedPrecedence) ranks by the grammar's precedences orders, the earlier entry higher, as tree-sitter's compare_precedence; a rule entry ranks every precedence of that rule's productions. A scanner's (expected ITEM) asks whether the parse requested a literal or a rule at the scanner's context offset, as a tree-sitter scanner asks valid_symbols; a parse whose answer was given before the request is run again with the requests so far. The tree-sitter importer keeps named precedences and the precedences orders instead of approximating them by level.
feat(grammar): the Rust codecs carry named precedences and their declared orders, and the expected scanner condition

feat(grammar): the Rust runtime ranks named precedences by the declared orders, as the JavaScript runtime does

A precedence carries its name and the rule whose body holds it; compare_precedence mirrors comparePrecedence (tree-sitter's compare_precedence), and shift_order, the lone and extra reductions, the chain conflict, the shift preference and the precedence filter rank by it. An extra reduction outside any node in progress now decides by its associativity, as in the JavaScript runtime.

feat(grammar): the Rust runtime answers a scanner's expected condition by what the parse requested, rerunning a stale parse, as the JavaScript runtime does

The layout feature of the grammar feature union fixture now exercises (expected ITEM) with a mutation whose outcome differs and two load errors (an undefined rule, an item that is neither a literal nor a rule). The feature union document describes named precedences, the precedences declaration and the expected condition.
chore(acceptance): the requirements manifest digests the grammar feature union fixture as committed

fix(grammar): native Rust builds the oracle rows of the formal-ai sources: keywords lexed only in the tree's parse state, the shift order compares where two parses part, and a node ending a silent rule keeps its reduction precedence, in both runtimes
refactor(grammar): the Rust token ranks of a longest-match grammar move from load.rs to token_ranks.rs, keeping load.rs under the 1000-line limit
fix(grammar): a scanner's token wins over a lexer's token, and an alias of an inline rule imports as the rule substituted, in both runtimes

fix(grammar): two nodes of one kind that part where a child of one was reduced alone to a ranked silent rule keep the shift by precedence, in both runtimes

JavaScript's `new f()` before a template now parses as tree-sitter does: the
new_expression shifts its arguments under `new`, where the call reduced `f` to
`expression`, which (precedences ... (name new) (name call) (rule expression))
ranks below `new`. An item a silent rule named by a `rule` entry of the
orders reduces alone records that rule (reducedAlone / reduced_alone), and
childParting / child_parting compares the shifting node's precedence against
that reduction's.

fix(grammar): two nodes of different kinds over the same tokens settle by precedence, and a leaf conflict waits for the lookahead only where one parse reduced the leaf, in both runtimes

JavaScript's `{}` and `{b}` parse as a statement_block where a statement is
expected, as tree-sitter parses them: the reduce/reduce conflict between the
block and an object over the same tokens is settled by the precedence they
are reduced with. A leaf one parse has alone against a node the other begins
with it puts the lexer's conflict off only where a silent rule reduced it
alone, or the node or one along its leftmost chain ends with it; a leaf a
silent rule reduced alone in one parse only parts the two at its end; and two
leaves of one span one token rule built (an identifier and its alias) are one
token. An item now records every ranked silent rule that reduced it alone.

The Rust helpers move to feature_runtime/parting.rs with child_parting,
keeping ordering.rs under the line limit. The JavaScript corpus agrees with
tree-sitter-javascript on 113 of 116 cases (from 111) and the two runtimes
build identical trees on all 116.

perf(grammar): a left-recursive call whose first pass has no result does not grow, in both runtimes

A second pass with the same empty seed only repeated the first; skipping it
roughly halves the steps of JavaScript's primary_expression chains, so the
corpus cases Functions and if/for/while/do statements without semicolons
fit the default step budget.

feat(grammar): import the pinned tree-sitter-javascript grammar with its native scanner

tree-sitter-javascript 0.25.0 is pinned with its corpus and license;
parity/grammars/scanners/javascript.lino ports src/scanner.c (automatic
semicolons, html comments, template characters and the ternary question
mark). The native grammar parses the 115 cases of the upstream corpus the
oracle accepts into the oracle's rows in both runtimes and rejects the one
the oracle recovers from. The naming decisions expand the JavaScript
abbreviations (chars, lhs, qmark, regex), share the argument list and
boolean value concepts, and register the ECMA-262 and JSX terms.

fix(incremental): an edit keeps the order of siblings that share a span

The network orders siblings by span, then identifier. apply_edit remapped a
reparsed link to its old identifier, or to its own when that was free, else
to a fresh one, so two zero-width MISSING leaves at one point (the class body
`{` `}` of a trailing JavaScript `class`) could swap. Where the remapped
identifiers would reverse siblings that share a span, the later one gets a
fresh identifier, so the edited network equals a fresh parse.

feat(grammar): parse JavaScript with the native merged grammar by default

JavaScript joins the native languages: parity/grammars/native/javascript.lino,
imported from the pinned tree-sitter-javascript 0.25.0 grammar with its
external scanner ported to five native scanners (automatic semicolons,
template characters, the ternary question mark, HTML-like comments and JSX
text), is the default JavaScript parse in both runtimes.

- parity/fixtures/native-grammars/javascript.json checks the grammar against
  the oracle on 146 matches (the 115 accepted upstream corpus cases and 31
  more) and 24 rejections, with no divergence; the ledger row
  I195-GRAMMAR-NATIVE-JAVASCRIPT tracks the JavaScript and Rust suites.
- The recovery suites cover the JavaScript rejections, and
  parity/fixtures/native-recovery.json records the 61 JavaScript conformance
  and generative cases whose recovered tree differs from tree-sitter's.
- A MISSING leaf for a literal under a lexical precedence (the closing `/` of
  an unterminated regular expression) carries the literal as its kind in both
  runtimes, and a kindless MISSING leaf projects to a named MISSING node in
  JavaScript as in Rust.
- The JavaScript scanner links lose a stray space before a closing
  parenthesis, so the grammar round-trips its concepts and source names.
- The catalogs, the grammar inventory, the shared concepts and concept reuse
  reports, and the native grammar docs list JavaScript.

build(grammar): tree-sitter-javascript is a development oracle only

The native merged grammar is the default JavaScript parse in both runtimes,
so the tree-sitter-javascript crate moves to [dev-dependencies], its
WebAssembly build and license move to js/oracles/grammars outside the npm
package, its lock entries carry "oracle": true and grammar_by_id no longer
maps "javascript". pinned_javascript_oracle_gives_the_fixture keeps checking
that the pinned oracle still gives the fixture rows.

feat(grammar): pin tree-sitter-typescript 0.23.2 sources and corpus

The pin script writes one grammar.json per grammar directory of a
repository (typescript, tsx), and the corpus splitter reads the
:language(NAME) attribute tree-sitter-typescript's shared corpus uses to
run a case on one of its grammars only.

feat(grammar): import TypeScript and TSX with a native port of their scanner

The importer reads the pinned tree-sitter-typescript 0.23.2 grammars, the
scanner port (common/scanner.h) is generated by
js/experiments/build-typescript-scanner.mjs, and naming decisions settle
the names that read the same natively. Not yet the default parse.

feat(grammar): merge TypeScript and TSX into the shared concepts

tree-sitter aliases each step of an aliased sequence, so TypeScript's
`unique symbol` is two leaves of that kind with no node over them; the
importer now distributes such an alias over the sequence. The merge
pipeline writes the TypeScript and TSX merge reports and their shared
concepts with JavaScript, C and Rust.

fix(grammar-runtime): shifts a reduction below decides, as in an LR parser

A shift whose precedence outranks the reduction a lower rule makes at the
same point wins (TypeScript's mapped type `as` clauses), and where the
shifting rule takes its first part only after reducing it to a silent rule
the two reductions conflict (`keyof U & V`), unless the rule takes the
part directly (JavaScript's `new module.Klass()`).

fix(grammar-runtime): a declared fork merges as tree-sitter's, and wrapped tokens are requested

A scanner's (expected ITEM) now sees a token the parse requests in a token
wrapper (TypeScript's (immediateToken (ref
function_signature_automatic_semicolon))), so `function foo()\n{}` is a
declaration. Two nodes over the same tokens whose parses forked at a
conflict the grammar declares are settled as ts_subtree_compare settles
them where the parses merge, by the rule defined first (`<A>(a): T => a`
is an arrow function with type parameters). TypeScript and TSX now give
the oracle's tree on all 111 cases of the pinned corpus.

fix(grammar-runtime): mirror the forked-conflict and shift-reduction rules in Rust

The Rust executor now settles the conflicts the JavaScript executor settles
since e7ec0a4 and 2cd0af3: shifts_below in the precedence filter, the
reduction before a shift (shift_reduction), the merge of two forks at a
declared conflict (forked_order, with the grammar's conflict groups and rule
order in GrammarFacts), and the request of a token's scanner item.

fix(grammar-runtime): fork at a declared shift-reduce conflict, as tree-sitter does

tree-sitter's handle_conflict compares a reduction with every item that would
shift the lookahead; when some rank above it and some below, the conflict is
left to the grammar's declared conflicts and the generated parser forks. Both
runtimes now do the same (declaredFork / declared_fork): from the FIRST sets of
the rules and the items after the part a left operand's rule ends with, the
precedence filter lets the reduced operand through, and the merge of the two
parses keeps the one that reduced it. TypeScript's `!g<T>()`, `await g<T>;`,
`typeof g<T>();` and the like now parse as tree-sitter-typescript parses them;
the JS and Rust runtimes give the same trees on all 111 TypeScript and 111 TSX
corpus cases, and the JavaScript, C and Rust grammar tests still pass.

fix(grammar-runtime): order TypeScript's declaration and expression readings as tree-sitter does

A pair of parses that reduced a node to different parents is ranked by the
rule each reduced to alone; an extra reduction is ranked against the rule
that owns the precedence; a reduction's closing precedence is that of the
last node it closed; and a zero-width scanned token that one parse takes
after a node both reduced decides for that parse, as tree-sitter's lexer
scans it before either reduces.
fix(grammar-runtime): mirror TypeScript's declaration and expression ordering in Rust

feat(grammar): parse TypeScript and TSX with the native merged grammars by default

TypeScript and TSX join the native languages: parity/grammars/native/typescript.lino
and parity/grammars/native/tsx.lino, imported from the pinned
tree-sitter-typescript 0.23.2 grammars with their shared external scanner
ported to seven native scanners, are the default TypeScript and TSX parses in
both runtimes.

- parity/fixtures/native-grammars/typescript.json checks the TypeScript grammar
  against the oracle on 155 matches (the 111 upstream corpus cases and 44 more)
  and 15 rejections, and tsx.json the TSX grammar on 157 matches (111 and 46
  more, JSX included) and 16 rejections, with no divergence and no ambiguity;
  the ledger rows I195-GRAMMAR-NATIVE-TYPESCRIPT and I195-GRAMMAR-NATIVE-TSX
  track the JavaScript and Rust suites.
- The recovery suites cover the TypeScript and TSX rejections; the conformance
  and generative corpora have no TypeScript or TSX case, so
  parity/fixtures/native-recovery.json gains no record.
- The concept records, the catalogs, the grammar inventory, the default CST
  expectations, the shared concepts and concept reuse reports, and the native
  grammar docs list TypeScript and TSX; 128 more concepts three or more native
  grammars name are shared constructs.

build(grammar): tree-sitter-typescript is a development oracle only

TypeScript and TSX parse with the native merged grammars by default, so the
pinned tree-sitter-typescript grammars move to js/oracles/grammars, which
the npm package does not ship, and the crate moves to [dev-dependencies].
grammar_by_id no longer has a typescript or tsx arm; only the pinned oracle
tests load them.
fix(naming): TypeScript and TSX concept names pass the naming gate
chore(issue-195): refresh the requirement manifest fixture hashes

test: the generative manifest records the current conformance manifest hash

752a270 moved the JavaScript oracle and changed the conformance manifest,
and the generative manifest kept the old hash.

fix(dependencies): the TypeScript and TSX oracle grammars are declared in the grammar lock

The inventory recorded js/oracles/grammars/grammar-lock.json, which does not
exist; the pinned oracle grammars stay in js/src/vendor/grammars/grammar-lock.json.

feat(evidence): publish the merge quality of every native grammar against its oracle

docs/grammar/merge-quality-evidence.md compares the 12 native grammars with
the pinned tree-sitter grammars they were merged from, on their corpora: the
upstream test corpus at the pinned revision for C, Rust, JavaScript,
TypeScript and TSX, and the curated cases for the others. It reports coverage
(rules by kind, visible rules exercised, checked kinds and fields, merge
report counts), preserved features (scanners, conflicts, precedences, extras,
kinds), correctness (matches, rows, bytes, divergences, rejections), recovery
(repairs, ERROR and MISSING nodes, recovery categories), shared reuse, and the
time and memory of the native executor and the oracle in both runtimes.

js/scripts/build-merge-quality-evidence.mjs writes the deterministic part to
parity/fixtures/merge-quality-evidence.json, which the JavaScript and Rust
suites recompute and compare; --measure measures each JavaScript side in its
own process and the Rust executor in the merge_quality test target, whose
counting allocator gives the peak of live heap bytes. npm run
check:merge-quality fails on drift, and CI runs it.

The native executors are 13x to 666x slower than the oracle in JavaScript and
114x to 1809x in the unoptimized Rust test profile; the report says so.

feat(grammar): pin tree-sitter-lean sources and corpus

wvhulle/tree-sitter-lean commits grammar.js and the generated parser.c,
not src/grammar.json: the pinned grammar.json is the one tree-sitter CLI
0.27.0 writes from grammar.js at bd942cd (its dsl.js, then serde_json's
pretty printing in insertion order), reproduced by
js/experiments/generate-tree-sitter-grammar-json.mjs. Every reachable
rule is a symbol of the vendored oracle's parser.c. The corpus is the
22 files of test/corpus at the same revision.

The importer's reviewed name and concept decisions are looked up as own
properties: tree-sitter-lean has a rule named constructor, which read
Object.prototype.constructor as its decided name.

feat(grammar): import tree-sitter-lean with a native layout scanner

The importer reads the pinned tree-sitter-lean4 0.3.0 grammar, the layout
scanner port (src/scanner.c) is generated by
js/experiments/build-lean-scanner.mjs, and a hidden immediate token is a
token tree-sitter leaves unnamed, as Lean's _string_content. Not yet the
default parse.

fix(grammar): the Lean layout scanner port has no error-recovery step

The native parse asks for one token at a time and `expected` is the union
over the parses in progress, so all three layout tokens can be expected
where no one parse expects them, as after `do do`. Of the Lean corpus
cases the oracle parses, eleven rejected ones now parse.

fix(grammar): the shift-reduce conflicts the Lean corpus shows are ranked as tree-sitter ranks them

A node both parses reduce alike on their leftmost chains parts them above it
(#check foo 2 3); a node the other result goes on past in a node of its own
conflicts as a shift against a reduction ((f x).y); and the chain conflict
descends into two last parts of one kind from one offset (g do return x) and
accepts a long part that begins with the short one (-x ^ 3 * 7).

fix(grammar): a child a silent rule captures keeps the innermost field over it, as tree-sitter names it

Lean's `∀ x : Nat, p` names `Nat` by the `type` field of its binder, not
by the `binders` field the silent rule that holds it captures it under.
Adds js/experiments/oracle-parse-log.mjs, the oracle's GLR parse log.

fix(grammar): two reductions of one handle a conflict declares are ranked as tree-sitter ranks them

Lean's `do return x` reduces the same children to a `return` and a
`do_return`, two reduce actions of one table entry the grammar declares a
conflict between. tree-sitter goes on with the version of the last reduce,
the rule defined later, and merges the other into it where both shift the
next token; where none but zero-width tokens follow, both are accepted and
the tree of the lower symbols is kept. Both runtimes now rank such a pair
so, and a chain conflict treats two such rules as one kind.

The Rust runtime also gets the fixes of the two previous commits: the
innermost field of a child a silent rule captures, the whole-chain skip and
the extra-reduction fallback of the shift order, and the chain-conflict
loop, moved to parting.rs with `shifted_past`.

fix(grammar): a fork at a silent rule a conflict declares is ranked as tree-sitter ranks it

Lean's `let x := 2` reduces `x` to a `pattern` in one parse (a `do_let`)
and shifts it as a `let` name in the other; the conflict tree-sitter-lean
declares between them now ranks the parses by rule order, as the oracle
does. Both runtimes record the silent rules a declared conflict names
(`forkedTo` / `forked_to`) and compare them in `forkedOrder`. The JS
scanner also gets an off-by-default trace hook (`globalThis.__scanTrace`).

fix(grammar): a token the external scanner scans of no width is taken where the scanner scans it

tree-sitter runs the external scanner before its lexer wherever its tokens
are valid, so a zero-width scanned token is the lookahead there. A
repetition iteration that takes such a token (Lean's layout semicolon
between two structure fields) is now a result; two parses where one built
nothing before such a token part at it (`preferredTokens` /
`scanned_after_end`); and `sameTokens` / `same_tokens` skip zero-width
scanned leaves. The JavaScript, TypeScript and TSX fixtures record the
automatic semicolon at the end of input in recovered trees, as the oracle
emits it; their accepted trees are unchanged.

fix(grammar): a parse a zero-width scanned token preempts is no parse

Where the item after a result begins with a token the external scanner
scans of no width (Lean's layout end after `12` in `def foo := 12` before
a line break), tree-sitter scans that token before it lexes, so a parse in
the same state that holds the same last token and lexes past it (`12
partial`, an application across the line break) is dropped, and a
repetition result such a token continues is no parse itself. The Lean
corpus now matches the oracle on all 218 cases it accepts, with linear
steps where the skipped layout ends multiplied the scanner states.

Rust: `ValueMachine` moves to operations.rs to keep executor.rs under the
file size limit. New experiments: native-fixture-diff.mjs,
native-default-recovery-diff.mjs and native-rule-profile.mjs.

feat(grammar): merge Lean into the shared concepts

The merge pipeline writes the Lean merge report (147 rules, no
approximation and no unsupported construct) and the concept records of
its rules, shared by name with the other native grammars.

fix(grammar): a repair is not repeated at its offset after a MISSING leaf zero-width scanned tokens follow

A MISSING leaf nested in a node and followed by tokens the external scanner
scanned of no width (a layout token opening an indented block) escaped the
chain guard, so each repaired Lean block opened another up to the scanner's
deepest indentation. The default step budget with error recovery is doubled,
since its rounds parse each repaired alternative too.

fix(grammar): a literal an immediate token takes is not lexed plainly where the immediate one is valid

Under (matching longest), tree-sitter lexes an immediate token over the
plain literal of the same text wherever both are valid, so Lean's
foo[1:2:3] opens a subscript, which fails at the second colon, rather than
applying foo to a range. KeywordLexing in both runtimes records the spans
where an immediate literal matched; a plain leaf of that text the tree took
in the same parse state makes the span immediate-only and the input is
parsed again. The ambiguity feature of the grammar feature union gains an
access rule that shows it, with a mutation that drops (matching longest).
docs(grammar): an immediate literal outranks the plain one in keyword lexing

fix(grammar): a silent rule one parse ends early and the other later is settled by its associativity

Where two results share a token but one closed a silent rule under a
precedence there and the other shifted on in that rule, a later item of
the other's node in progress that closes with the same rule and
precedence makes the pair that rule reduced from one offset and ending
apart: right associativity keeps the shift, left the reduction (Lean's
set_option pp.all true).
fix(ci): group the merge quality evidence test with the tooling tests
feat(grammar): Lean parses natively by default with shared concepts and readable names

fix(grammar): a zero-width scanned token does not hide the parse state of a keyword

Records the native recoveries of JavaScript and Lean anew with
generate-native-recovery.mjs.
chore(experiments): probe the Lean sources the native grammar and the oracle read apart

body:
## Progress on the green-path audit: Lean native by default, and the JavaScript `class` keyword fix (`fe9b6ff`)

Pushed:
- `5415a3f`: the merge quality evidence test now belongs to the tooling group, which fixes the JS CI test-groups check.
- `266f450`: Lean parses natively by default.
  - The merged grammar uses shared concepts and readable rule names, such as `instance_declaration` and `tactic_sequence`.
  - New requirement `I195-GRAMMAR-NATIVE-LEAN`, with JS and Rust suites.
  - The naming gate is clean.
  - The concept records, catalogs and default CST fixture are regenerated.
- `3d8b5f4`: root cause of the Rust CI failures in `link_network` and `issue_195_generative_javascript`.
  - `treeReach` / `TreeReach::of` counted the zero-width automatic semicolon as a tree leaf.
  - As a result, a keyword `class` after `x\n` was treated as outside the parse state and lexed as an identifier.
  - Fixed in both runtimes, with regression cases (`x\nclass`, `\nfunction foo() {}\nclass`).
  - The native recoveries are re-recorded.

Verified locally:

| Runtime | Passing |
| --- | --- |
| JS | native JavaScript/TypeScript/TSX/Lean/recovery suites, `error-recovery-parity`, and the JavaScript/Rust/Rocq generative cases |
| Rust | `link_network`, `issue_195_grammar_native_lean`, `issue_195_grammar_native_javascript`, and `issue_195_generative` except Lean |

Still failing in both runtimes: Lean generative `edit/6`, steps 1 to 3.
- The oracle reads `mport Lism.SemanticTableau.InfoTreeParser` as an application of `mport` to the dotted name.
- The native grammar reads it as a projection of `(mport Lism)`.
- This is the dotted-name ambiguity that associativity settled for `set_option pp.all true`, now inside an application argument.
- `js/experiments/lean-edit6.mjs` probes it.
- `generate-native-recovery.mjs Lean` also reports `corpus/functions.txt/6` (the merged `@foo.bar` divergence) and `project/StateRef.lean`, which the oracle parses cleanly but the native grammar does not.

Next: fix those Lean trees, then make the Lean oracle dev-only, then Rocq, then the families.

### 3. Not started yet, and required in this PR

1. **The JavaScript → Rust CI order.**
   - No Rust job may start until every JavaScript job has passed. Use one workflow with `needs:`, or trigger `rust.yml` with `workflow_run` on a successful `js.yml`; keep the check names the ruleset requires valid.
   - The same order applies to the acceptance workflow's stages.
   - Rust jobs skipped because JavaScript failed show as skipped.
   - A repository test enforces all of this.
2. **Report every failure in one run:**
   - `cargo test --no-fail-fast`;
   - `if: ${{ !cancelled() }}` on every check step, or one script that runs all checks and reports every failure at the end;
   - independent fmt, clippy and doc steps;
   - a workflow-structure test.
3. **The self-translation tool**, as a library API and CLI in both packages.
   - It reads JavaScript/TypeScript into meta-language links and writes Rust, and the reverse.
   - Use it to port `js/src` to `rust/src` instead of hand-mirroring commits. Generated Rust passes `cargo check`, clippy and the shared parity corpus.
   - Round trips: lossless same-language, behavior-preserving across languages.
   - Meta-language's own source is the acceptance corpus.
   - Follow the [RML PR #184](https://github.com/link-foundation/relative-meta-logic/pull/184) pattern: shared corpus cases with expected outputs written in Links Notation and checked in both runtimes.
   - `parity/language-features.json` must be complete, and a test must fail on any feature missing in Rust.
4. **Decorators at every level:** importer, grammar rule, merge decision, concept mapping, executor and recovery, CST → AST, transformation, emitter, translation rule.
   - They compose in a defined order and are stored as links data shared by both runtimes.
   - They are used to make translated output match the existing hand-written source, with the difference per module measured and published.
   - Tests cover each level, composition order and removal.
